options.a: Begin high-quality CPR and use an AED as soon as available
options.b: Call for help and wait for EMS before starting compressions
options.c: Start with 2 rescue breaths, then begin compressions at 30:2
options.d: Check a pulse for up to 30 seconds before starting compressions

distractorExplanations.b: Waiting for EMS delays compressions; every minute without CPR lowers the chance of survival.
distractorExplanations.c: Breaths-first (A-B-C) is the old sequence; current AHA adult CPR starts with compressions (C-A-B).
distractorExplanations.d: Pulse checks are limited to no more than 10 seconds before starting CPR, not up to 30 seconds.

aha-bls-provider-readiness-check-adult-c.explanation: Adult cardiac arrest care prioritizes immediate compressions (starting CPR with chest compressions) and early defibrillation.

options.a: 1 inch (2.5 cm), not exceeding about 1.5 inches (4 cm)
options.b: 1.5 inches (4 cm), not exceeding about 2 inches (5 cm)
options.c: 2 inches (5 cm), not exceeding about 2.4 inches (6 cm)
options.d: 3 inches (7.5 cm), not exceeding about 3.5 inches (9 cm)

distractorExplanations.a: One inch is far too shallow; adult compressions need a depth of at least 2 inches (5 cm).
distractorExplanations.b: About 1.5 inches (4 cm) is the infant depth target; adults need at least 2 inches (5 cm).
distractorExplanations.d: Three inches exceeds the 2.4-inch (6 cm) upper limit for adults and raises the risk of injury.

options.a: Keeping light pressure on the sternum between compressions
options.b: Lifting the hands fully off the chest after each compression
options.c: Pausing about 2 seconds after each compression so the chest refills
options.d: Letting the chest return to normal position between compressions

distractorExplanations.a: Residual pressure (leaning) prevents full recoil and reduces venous return to the heart.
distractorExplanations.b: Hands stay in contact with the chest; lifting off risks losing hand position and bouncing.
distractorExplanations.c: Recoil happens within each compression cycle at 100-120/min; deliberate pauses drop the rate.

aha-bls-provider-readiness-check-adult-c.explanation: Leaning reduces venous return; full recoil without leaning between compressions improves CPR quality.

options.a: Complete 5 cycles of CPR before attaching the pads
options.b: Power on the AED, apply pads, and follow prompts
options.c: Place both pads side by side on the left chest
options.d: Attach the pads and keep compressing while it analyzes

distractorExplanations.a: Current guidance is to use the AED as soon as it arrives, not after a fixed number of CPR cycles.
distractorExplanations.c: Pads go in anterolateral (right upper chest, left side) or anteroposterior positions, not side by side.
distractorExplanations.d: Everyone must stand clear while the AED analyzes; compressions resume after the shock or no-shock prompt.

aha-bls-provider-readiness-check-adult-c.explanation: Early defibrillation is critical for shockable rhythms; minimize pauses and resume CPR immediately after a shock or no-shock advice.

options.a: Check for a pulse for 10 seconds before resuming CPR
options.b: Give 2 rescue breaths, then reassess breathing
options.c: Resume CPR immediately starting with compressions
options.d: Turn off the AED and continue rescue breathing only

distractorExplanations.a: After a no-shock prompt, resume compressions at once; rhythm and pulse are rechecked after about 2 minutes.
distractorExplanations.b: Breaths-first delays compressions; after the prompt, CPR resumes starting with compressions.
distractorExplanations.d: Pads and AED stay on to reanalyze every 2 minutes; a pulseless patient needs compressions, not breaths alone.

options.a: Heel of one hand on the upper half of the sternum, other on top
options.b: Heel of one hand on the xiphoid process, other hand on top
options.c: Two fingers on the sternum just below the nipple line
options.d: Heel of one hand on the center of the chest, other hand on top

distractorExplanations.a: The upper sternum is too high; compress on the lower half of the sternum in the center of the chest.
distractorExplanations.b: Pressing on the xiphoid can injure the liver; hands go on the lower half of the sternum above it.
distractorExplanations.c: Fingertip compressions below the nipple line are an infant technique; adults need two hands.

aha-bls-provider-readiness-check-adult-c.explanation: Correct hand position (heel of one hand on the lower half of the sternum, other hand on top) maximizes effective compressions and reduces injury risk.

options.a: Coordinate roles and switch compressors about every 2 minutes
options.b: Check a pulse after every cycle of 30 compressions and 2 breaths
options.c: Switch compressors only when the first rescuer feels tired
options.d: Stop compressions while the AED pads are being applied

distractorExplanations.b: Pulse checks every cycle create frequent pauses; checks happen about every 2 minutes at rhythm analysis.
distractorExplanations.c: Fatigue lowers quality before rescuers notice it, so compressors switch about every 2 minutes.
distractorExplanations.d: Compressions continue while pads are applied; pause when the AED analyzes or delivers a shock.

aha-bls-provider-readiness-check-adult-c.explanation: High chest compression fraction improves outcomes; limit pulse/rhythm checks, and brief planned switches beat long chaotic pauses.

options.a: Be delivered over about 3 seconds each to fill the lungs
options.b: Produce visible chest rise over about 1 second each
options.c: Fill the lungs until the abdomen visibly rises
options.d: Be given as 10 breaths before starting compressions

distractorExplanations.a: Each breath should last about 1 second; longer breaths lengthen pauses in compressions.
distractorExplanations.c: Abdominal rise signals gastric inflation; give just enough volume for visible chest rise.
distractorExplanations.d: Prolonged breath-first sequences delay compressions; adult CPR uses 30:2 starting with compressions.

aha-bls-provider-readiness-check-adult-c.explanation: Overventilation increases intrathoracic pressure and decreases venous return; avoid excessive ventilation.

options.a: Start CPR for 2 minutes before calling EMS or getting an AED
options.b: Check a pulse for 30 seconds, then call EMS and start CPR
options.c: Check responsiveness, activate EMS/get AED, then start CPR
options.d: Check responsiveness, give 2 breaths, then activate EMS

distractorExplanations.a: Two minutes of CPR before calling is for a lone rescuer with an unwitnessed child or infant arrest, not a witnessed adult collapse.
distractorExplanations.b: Pulse checks are limited to 10 seconds; a 30-second check delays EMS activation and compressions.
distractorExplanations.d: Breaths before activating EMS delay help and the AED; adult CPR then starts with compressions.

aha-bls-provider-readiness-check-adult-c.explanation: Rapid EMS activation and AED retrieval are core adult Chain of Survival links; ensure scene safety and check responsiveness and breathing first.

options.a: Place the pad directly over the patch to save time
options.b: Delay the AED until EMS removes the patch safely
options.c: Wipe the patch with an alcohol pad and place the pad over it
options.d: Remove the patch and wipe the area dry

distractorExplanations.a: A pad over a medication patch can block energy delivery and cause skin burns.
distractorExplanations.b: Rescuers remove the patch themselves; waiting for EMS loses defibrillation time.
distractorExplanations.c: Wiping the surface does not remove the patch; it can still block current and cause burns.

aha-bls-provider-readiness-check-adult-c.explanation: Patches can block energy and burn skin; remove the patch and wipe residue dry before applying the pad.

options.a: Breathing adequately—place in the recovery position and monitor
options.b: Not breathing normally—start CPR if unresponsive and pulseless
options.c: Seizure activity—protect the head and wait for it to stop
options.d: An airway obstruction—begin abdominal thrusts at once

distractorExplanations.a: Agonal gasps are not normal breathing; the recovery position would delay needed CPR.
distractorExplanations.c: Gasping and brief jerking can follow cardiac arrest; treat it as not breathing, not as a seizure.
distractorExplanations.d: Agonal gasps signal cardiac arrest, not choking; abdominal thrusts are for responsive choking victims.

options.a: 30 seconds (or at each pause for breaths)
options.b: 1 minute (or sooner if the compressor feels tired)
options.c: 2 minutes (or when prompted by AED/team leader)
options.d: 5 minutes (or when the AED prompts a shock)

distractorExplanations.a: Switching every 30 seconds adds needless pauses; the standard interval is about 2 minutes.
distractorExplanations.b: Fatigue degrades quality before rescuers notice it; switch about every 2 minutes, not by feel.
distractorExplanations.d: Five minutes is too long; depth and rate fall off within about 2 minutes of compressing.

aha-bls-provider-readiness-check-adult-c.explanation: Fatigue quickly degrades depth and rate; planned switches about every 2 minutes reduce fatigue and maintain quality.

options.a: About one-third the depth of the chest, approximately 2 inches (5 cm)
options.b: Shallow enough to avoid rib fractures, about one-quarter of the chest
options.c: The same 2.4-inch (6 cm) minimum used for adult compressions
options.d: About one-half the depth of the chest, approximately 3 inches (7.5 cm)

distractorExplanations.b: Fear of rib fractures leads to shallow compressions; children need about one-third of chest depth.
distractorExplanations.c: 2.4 inches (6 cm) is the adult upper limit, not a minimum; children need about 2 inches (5 cm).
distractorExplanations.d: One-half of chest depth is too deep and risks injury; the pediatric target is about one-third.

options.a: The heel of both hands stacked, as for an adult victim
options.b: Two thumbs pressing on the xiphoid with hands around the chest
options.c: Two fingers (1 rescuer) or two-thumb–encircling hands (2 rescuers)
options.d: Two fingers placed on the upper third of the sternum

distractorExplanations.a: Two stacked hands are an adult technique and would compress an infant chest far too deeply.
distractorExplanations.b: Thumbs go just below the nipple line on the lower sternum, not on the xiphoid process.
distractorExplanations.d: Infant compressions are on the lower half of the sternum, just below the nipple line, not the upper third.

options.a: 0.5 inch (1 cm)
options.b: 0.75 inch (2 cm)
options.c: 1 inch (2.5 cm)
options.d: 1.5 inches (4 cm)

distractorExplanations.a: Half an inch is far too shallow to generate blood flow; infants need about 1.5 inches (4 cm).
distractorExplanations.b: Three-quarters of an inch is too shallow; the infant target is about one-third chest depth, 1.5 inches.
distractorExplanations.c: One inch underestimates the target; infant compressions should be about 1.5 inches (4 cm), one-third of chest depth.

options.a: Activate EMS/get AED if not already done, then continue CPR
options.b: Continue CPR without pausing until EMS arrives at the scene
options.c: Check a pulse for 30 seconds before deciding to call EMS
options.d: Give 5 back blows, then continue CPR before calling EMS

distractorExplanations.b: No one has called EMS yet; after about 2 minutes of CPR the lone rescuer must activate EMS.
distractorExplanations.c: Pulse checks are limited to 10 seconds; a 30-second check delays EMS activation and CPR.
distractorExplanations.d: Back blows are for a responsive choking infant, not an unwitnessed arrest; the next step is EMS.

options.a: Sudden ventricular fibrillation than respiratory failure or shock
options.b: Respiratory problems / hypoxia than primary sudden cardiac causes
options.c: Congenital heart rhythm disorders than airway problems
options.d: Commotio cordis from chest impact than respiratory causes

distractorExplanations.a: VF is less common in children; most pediatric arrests follow respiratory failure or shock.
distractorExplanations.c: Congenital rhythm disorders cause some arrests, but respiratory failure and hypoxia are more common.
distractorExplanations.d: Commotio cordis is rare; pediatric arrest usually follows progressive respiratory failure.

aha-bls-provider-readiness-check-child-i.explanation: Pediatric arrest is more often preceded by respiratory problems/hypoxia than primary sudden cardiac causes, though both occur; the Pediatric Chain of Survival emphasizes prevention and oxygenation, and compressions are still given for pulseless arrest.

options.a: Be quick cheek puffs without watching for chest rise
options.b: Fill the infant's lungs until the abdomen rises
options.c: Be delivered over about 3 seconds each
options.d: Be gentle enough to produce chest rise

distractorExplanations.a: Breaths are judged by visible chest rise; puffs without watching risk giving too little or too much.
distractorExplanations.b: Abdominal rise signals gastric inflation; give just enough volume for visible chest rise.
distractorExplanations.c: Each breath takes about 1 second; longer breaths add pauses and risk overinflation.

aha-bls-provider-readiness-check-child-i.explanation: Overventilation is harmful; visible chest rise is the guide. With mouth-to-mouth-and-nose, the rescuer's mouth covers the infant's mouth and nose.

options.a: Full CPR at 15:2 now, since the child is unresponsive and not breathing
options.b: Rescue breathing, and start compressions if pulse remains <60 with poor perfusion
options.c: Rescue breathing at 1 breath every 6 seconds, starting compressions only if pulse is lost
options.d: Recovery position and monitoring until EMS arrives, with no breaths given

distractorExplanations.a: With a pulse of 60 or more, give rescue breaths; compressions start if it falls below 60 with poor perfusion.
distractorExplanations.c: Pediatric rescue breathing is 1 breath every 2-3 seconds, and compressions start below 60 with poor perfusion, not on pulse loss.
distractorExplanations.d: A child who is not breathing normally needs rescue breaths; the recovery position is for adequate breathing.

aha-bls-provider-readiness-check-child-i.explanation: Pediatric bradycardia with poor perfusion is a compression indication even if a pulse is present but too slow; give rescue breathing with pulse checks per AHA pediatric guidance.

options.a: 40 to 60 per minute
options.b: 60 to 80 per minute
options.c: 80 to 100 per minute
options.d: 100 to 120 per minute

distractorExplanations.a: 40-60/min sits near the bradycardia threshold for starting compressions; it is not a compression rate.
distractorExplanations.b: 60-80/min is too slow; infants and children get the same 100-120/min rate as adults.
distractorExplanations.c: 80-100/min is below target; the pediatric compression rate matches adults at 100-120/min.

options.a: Protect airway, place recovery position if appropriate, and monitor
options.b: Begin chest compressions because a seizure can stop the heart
options.c: Place a bite block in the mouth to protect the tongue
options.d: Give sips of water to prevent dehydration once the seizure has ended

distractorExplanations.b: Compressions are for pulseless arrest or poor perfusion; this child has a pulse and adequate breathing.
distractorExplanations.c: Nothing goes in a postictal child's mouth; objects can break teeth or block the airway.
distractorExplanations.d: Oral fluids after a seizure risk aspiration until the child is fully alert with a protected airway.

aha-bls-provider-readiness-check-child-i.explanation: CPR is for arrest/poor perfusion states; postictal care is supportive: protect the airway, monitor, and activate EMS as indicated by condition and history.

options.a: On the lower tip of the sternum (xiphoid)
options.b: Just below the nipple line on the sternum
options.c: On the upper third of the sternum near the neck
options.d: On the left chest over the heart

distractorExplanations.a: Pressing on the xiphoid risks liver injury; compress just below the nipple line on the sternum.
distractorExplanations.c: The upper sternum is too high; infant compressions use the lower half of the sternum.
distractorExplanations.d: Compressions go on the sternum, not the left chest; the heart is compressed between sternum and spine.

options.a: Cut adult pads in half so both fit on the front of the chest
options.b: Overlap the pads slightly so both fit on the front of the chest
options.c: Ensure pads do not touch (use AP placement if needed on small chests)
options.d: Skip the AED for children under 8 years if pediatric pads are not available

distractorExplanations.a: Pads must not be cut; use pediatric pads, or adult pads in anteroposterior position if needed.
distractorExplanations.b: Touching or overlapping pads can arc current; use anteroposterior placement instead.
distractorExplanations.d: If pediatric pads or an attenuator are unavailable, use adult pads; do not skip the AED.

aha-bls-provider-readiness-check-child-i.explanation: Pad contact and separation matter for effective, safe defibrillation; follow manufacturer guidance and use AP placement on small chests.

options.a: Abdominal thrusts until object expels or victim becomes unresponsive
options.b: Encouraging forceful coughing and waiting for the object to clear itself
options.c: A blind finger sweep to find the object, then abdominal thrusts
options.d: Rescue breaths to push the object past the airway

distractorExplanations.b: Coughing is encouraged in mild obstruction; inability to speak or cough means severe obstruction needing thrusts.
distractorExplanations.c: Blind finger sweeps can push the object deeper; remove an object only if you can see it.
distractorExplanations.d: Rescue breaths are given to an unresponsive victim within CPR; a responsive choking adult needs thrusts.

options.a: Continue abdominal thrusts with the victim lying on the back
options.b: Lower to a firm surface, begin CPR, and look for an object before breaths
options.c: Do a blind finger sweep, then give 2 breaths before compressions
options.d: Place in the recovery position and wait for EMS to clear the blocked airway

distractorExplanations.a: Supine abdominal thrusts are no longer taught; an unresponsive choking victim gets CPR.
distractorExplanations.c: Blind sweeps can push the object deeper, and a breaths-first sequence delays compressions.
distractorExplanations.d: An unresponsive choking victim is not breathing effectively; start CPR rather than recovery position.

aha-bls-provider-readiness-check-choking.explanation: Unresponsive choking transitions to CPR; look in the mouth before breaths and remove visible objects only, with no blind sweeps.

options.a: 5 back blows followed by 5 abdominal thrusts
options.b: 5 chest thrusts followed by 5 abdominal thrusts
options.c: 5 back blows followed by 5 chest thrusts
options.d: 5 back blows followed by a blind finger sweep

distractorExplanations.a: Abdominal thrusts can injure an infant's liver; infants get back blows and chest thrusts.
distractorExplanations.b: Abdominal thrusts are not used in infants; the sequence starts with 5 back blows.
distractorExplanations.d: Blind finger sweeps can push the object deeper in an infant; remove only visible objects.

aha-bls-provider-readiness-check-choking.explanation: Infant FBAO uses back blows and chest thrusts, not abdominal thrusts; repeat until relieved or the infant becomes unresponsive.

options.a: Pregnant or markedly obese responsive adults
options.b: Responsive children aged 1 year to puberty
options.c: Adults with a mild cough who can still speak
options.d: Elderly adults with a history of heart disease

distractorExplanations.b: Children from 1 year to puberty get abdominal thrusts like adults; chest thrusts are for infants and special cases.
distractorExplanations.c: A mild obstruction with an effective cough needs encouragement to cough, not thrusts.
distractorExplanations.d: Age and cardiac history do not change technique; chest thrusts are for pregnancy or marked obesity.

options.a: Chest compressions at 30:2 because naloxone takes time to act
options.b: Rescue breathing and naloxone per local protocols, plus EMS activation
options.c: Naloxone alone, then the recovery position while waiting for EMS
options.d: Rescue breaths only after naloxone has failed to work within 5 minutes

distractorExplanations.a: With a pulse present, the priority is ventilation; compressions start if the pulse is lost.
distractorExplanations.c: Naloxone does not replace ventilation; an apneic patient with a pulse needs rescue breaths.
distractorExplanations.d: Rescue breathing starts at once; waiting for naloxone to act leaves the patient hypoxic.

aha-bls-provider-readiness-check-choking.explanation: Opioid toxicity causes respiratory depression; support breathing (rescue breathing/ventilatory support) and use naloxone when indicated/available.

options.a: Give naloxone first and wait 2 minutes before starting CPR
options.b: Give rescue breaths and naloxone, but skip the AED in an overdose arrest
options.c: Start CPR and use AED; administer naloxone without delaying compressions
options.d: Start CPR but withhold the AED until naloxone has been given

distractorExplanations.a: In pulseless arrest CPR starts at once; naloxone must not delay compressions.
distractorExplanations.b: Opioid-associated arrests can have shockable rhythms; use the AED as in any arrest.
distractorExplanations.d: The AED is applied as soon as it arrives; naloxone must not delay defibrillation.

aha-bls-provider-readiness-check-choking.explanation: Cardiac arrest care still follows CPR/AED; naloxone is adjunctive, given as soon as available, and is not a reason to skip BLS.

options.a: Reverse low blood sugar in a person found unresponsive
options.b: Permanently reverse an overdose so EMS is not needed
options.c: Reverse respiratory depression from any sedative drug
options.d: Temporarily reverse opioid-induced respiratory depression

distractorExplanations.a: Low blood sugar is treated with glucose; naloxone reverses opioid effects, not hypoglycemia.
distractorExplanations.b: Naloxone wears off, often before the opioid does, so EMS care is still needed.
distractorExplanations.c: Naloxone is opioid-specific; it does not reverse benzodiazepines, alcohol, or other sedatives.

options.a: Become agitated or re-sedate later as naloxone wears off
options.b: Be released without EMS once awake for 15 minutes
options.c: Stay alert, since naloxone lasts longer than most opioids do
options.d: Safely drive home once breathing returns to normal

distractorExplanations.b: Re-sedation can occur after naloxone wears off; the person needs ongoing observation and EMS care.
distractorExplanations.c: Naloxone's effect often ends before long-acting opioids do, so re-sedation is a real risk.
distractorExplanations.d: Re-sedation can follow as naloxone wears off; the person should not drive and needs observation.

aha-bls-provider-readiness-check-choking.explanation: Renarcotization is a known risk; observation is mandatory, so continue observation and EMS care.

options.a: Abdominal thrusts while kneeling astride the child
options.b: CPR with checks for visible objects before breaths
options.c: Back blows and chest thrusts while lying on the floor
options.d: Blind finger sweeps before each set of compressions

distractorExplanations.a: Astride abdominal thrusts are not taught; an unresponsive choking child gets CPR.
distractorExplanations.c: Back blows and chest thrusts are for responsive choking infants, not an unresponsive child.
distractorExplanations.d: Blind sweeps can push the object deeper; remove only objects you can see.

options.a: Loud forceful coughing with the ability to speak in full sentences
options.b: Noisy wheezing between strong, effective coughs
options.c: Inability to speak, weak/silent cough, universal choking sign
options.d: Hoarse voice, strong cough, and normal skin color

distractorExplanations.a: Forceful coughing and full speech mean air is moving: mild obstruction, so encourage coughing.
distractorExplanations.b: Wheezing between effective coughs indicates mild obstruction; keep encouraging the victim to cough.
distractorExplanations.d: A strong cough with normal color and voice is mild obstruction; severe means no effective air movement.

aha-bls-provider-readiness-check-choking.explanation: Differentiate mild vs severe to choose observation vs thrusts; severe signs also include cyanosis.

options.a: Just above the navel, below the ribs
options.b: On the xiphoid process
options.c: Upper third of the sternum
options.d: Center of the sternum

distractorExplanations.a: Just above the navel is the abdominal-thrust position, which compresses the gravid uterus.
distractorExplanations.b: Pressing on the xiphoid risks liver injury; chest thrusts use the center of the sternum.
distractorExplanations.c: The upper sternum is too high; hands go on the center of the sternum, like CPR compressions.

aha-bls-provider-readiness-check-choking.explanation: Chest thrusts avoid the gravid abdomen; hands go in the same general area as CPR compressions, per BLS training details.

options.a: Use PPE as trained and avoid needle sticks
options.b: Delaying care until hazmat clears skin-contact risk
options.c: Wearing an N95 respirator before touching the victim
options.d: Recapping found needles before moving the victim

distractorExplanations.b: Incidental skin contact with fentanyl is very low risk; delaying care for hazmat costs critical time.
distractorExplanations.c: Routine respirators are not needed for overdose response; standard PPE and sharps care suffice.
distractorExplanations.d: Recapping needles is a leading cause of needle-stick injury; leave sharps alone or use a sharps container.

aha-bls-provider-readiness-check-choking.explanation: Rescuers protect themselves while providing rapid care; know fentanyl exposure myths vs real risks. Incidental skin contact is not the main danger; avoid mucous membrane/sharps exposure.

options.a: Done by any BLS rescuer with an airway kit
options.b: Left to trained ALS providers
options.c: Started before chest compressions begin
options.d: Given priority over early AED use

distractorExplanations.a: Advanced airways need ALS training and credentials; BLS uses bag-mask or mouth-to-mask ventilation.
distractorExplanations.c: Compressions come first; advanced airway placement must not delay CPR.
distractorExplanations.d: Early defibrillation outranks advanced airway placement in the BLS sequence.

aha-bls-provider-readiness-check-choking.explanation: Know your scope; BLS focuses on basic ventilation and compressions, and high-quality BLS bridges to ALS.

options.a: Switch to rescue breaths to force the object down
options.b: Stop thrusts and wait for EMS while the victim coughs
options.c: Continue cycles of thrusts until the object is expelled
options.d: Try a blind finger sweep after each unsuccessful round of thrusts

distractorExplanations.a: Rescue breaths are for unresponsive victims during CPR; a responsive victim needs continued thrusts.
distractorExplanations.b: A victim who cannot cough effectively needs ongoing thrusts, not waiting for EMS.
distractorExplanations.d: Blind sweeps can push the object deeper; look for and remove only visible objects.

aha-bls-provider-readiness-check-choking.explanation: Persist with the choking algorithm until the object is expelled; prepare to transition to CPR if the victim becomes unresponsive.

options.a: The receiver repeats back the order and the sender confirms
options.b: The sender repeats the order twice so everyone hears it
options.c: The receiver nods and starts the task without speaking
options.d: Each team member reports status to the leader at set intervals

distractorExplanations.b: Repeating an order is one-way; closed loop needs the receiver to echo it and the sender to confirm.
distractorExplanations.c: A nod gives no verbal check; closed loop requires a read-back and confirmation.
distractorExplanations.d: Scheduled reports are status updates; closed loop confirms each order as it is given.

options.a: Doing chest compressions personally while directing the team
options.b: Assigning roles, monitoring CPR quality, and summarizing the plan
options.c: Managing the airway while directing the other roles
options.d: Waiting for team members to choose their own roles

distractorExplanations.a: The leader stays hands-off to oversee the whole resuscitation and CPR quality.
distractorExplanations.c: Airway management is a team member role; a hands-on leader loses oversight.
distractorExplanations.d: The leader assigns roles; letting members self-select causes gaps and duplication.

options.a: Report the error to the team leader at the debrief afterward
options.b: Quietly correct the error without telling the leader
options.c: Speak up clearly if a critical error is about to occur
options.d: Wait until the leader asks for team input

distractorExplanations.a: Critical errors must be addressed in real time; the debrief is too late to protect the patient.
distractorExplanations.b: Silent corrections bypass the leader and closed-loop communication; state the concern clearly.
distractorExplanations.d: Waiting for permission lets an unsafe action happen; speak up immediately.

aha-bls-provider-readiness-check-team-sp.explanation: Safety culture expects respectful challenge of dangerous actions; speak up when a critical error or unsafe action is about to occur.

options.a: 2 breaths after every 15 compressions, pausing for each
options.b: 2 breaths after every 30 compressions, as without an airway
options.c: 1 breath every 6 seconds, pausing compressions for each
options.d: 1 breath every 6 seconds with continuous compressions

distractorExplanations.a: 15:2 with pauses is two-rescuer child/infant CPR without an advanced airway.
distractorExplanations.b: 30:2 is for CPR without an advanced airway; with one in place, compressions are continuous.
distractorExplanations.c: With an advanced airway, compressions do not pause for breaths; ventilation is asynchronous.

aha-bls-provider-readiness-check-team-sp.explanation: An advanced airway allows continuous compressions with timed breaths: 1 breath every 6 seconds (10/min) without 30:2 pauses.

options.a: Perform manual left uterine displacement to relieve aortocaval compression
options.b: Perform manual right uterine displacement to relieve vena cava pressure
options.c: Withhold AED shocks to protect the fetus until obstetric help arrives
options.d: Move hand position 2 inches lower on the sternum for compressions

distractorExplanations.b: Displacement is to the left, moving the uterus off the aorta and inferior vena cava.
distractorExplanations.c: Defibrillation is safe and indicated in pregnancy; withholding shocks harms mother and fetus.
distractorExplanations.d: Compression hand position is the same as for other adults, on the lower half of the sternum.

aha-bls-provider-readiness-check-team-sp.explanation: LUD improves venous return when the uterus is clinically significant; defibrillation is still indicated when needed; maternal resuscitation prioritizes CPR.

options.a: Keep going until the 2-minute rhythm check, then switch
options.b: Announce the need to switch and rotate immediately
options.c: Slow the rate to 90 per minute to keep the depth
options.d: Use one hand to rest the other while compressing

distractorExplanations.a: A fatigued compressor delivers shallow compressions; switch now rather than waiting for the check.
distractorExplanations.c: Rate must stay at 100-120/min; trading rate for depth still lowers CPR quality.
distractorExplanations.d: Adult compressions need two hands to reach adequate depth; resting one hand reduces depth further.

aha-bls-provider-readiness-check-team-sp.explanation: Teamwork corrects fatigue; announce the switch and rotate with minimal pause, since pride should not degrade CPR quality.

options.a: Squeezing the bag fully and quickly for each breath
options.b: One-rescuer use, which gives the best mask seal
options.c: Proper seal and often two-person technique
options.d: A mask sized to cover the chin and the eyes

distractorExplanations.a: Full, fast squeezes overinflate and cause gastric inflation; give just enough for chest rise over 1 second.
distractorExplanations.b: Two-rescuer bag-mask ventilation gives a better seal than the one-rescuer technique.
distractorExplanations.d: The mask covers the nose and mouth, from the bridge of the nose to the cleft of the chin, not the eyes.

aha-bls-provider-readiness-check-team-sp.explanation: Seal and airway position determine tidal delivery; two-person technique gives better ventilation. Avoid overventilation.

options.a: Move the victim to a firm surface
options.b: Compress harder to make up for the soft mattress
options.c: Switch to rescue breaths until a backboard arrives
options.d: Compress at a faster rate to offset the mattress

distractorExplanations.b: Extra force on a soft surface is absorbed by the mattress; firm support is needed for effective depth.
distractorExplanations.c: Compressions must continue; moving to a firm surface takes priority over breaths-only care.
distractorExplanations.d: A faster rate does not fix lost depth on a mattress; 100-120/min stays the target rate.

aha-bls-provider-readiness-check-team-sp.explanation: Soft surfaces dissipate force; move the victim to a firm surface or place a backboard if available to improve compression effectiveness.

options.a: Press the pads firmly over the hair and analyze
options.b: Quickly remove hair in the pad area so pads adhere
options.c: Move both pads to the back where there is less hair
options.d: Delay the AED and continue CPR until EMS arrives

distractorExplanations.a: Pads over thick hair make poor contact, causing failed analysis or skin burns.
distractorExplanations.c: Both pads on the back do not create a correct current path through the heart.
distractorExplanations.d: Delaying defibrillation lowers survival; clear the hair and use the AED.

aha-bls-provider-readiness-check-team-sp.explanation: Pad contact is required for AED function; kits often include a razor, so remove hair in the pad area, then analyze.

options.a: Apply the pads to the wet chest, as AEDs are water-safe
options.b: Dry only the pad sites, leaving the victim in the water
options.c: Move to a dry area if possible and dry the chest
options.d: Turn the victim onto the side to drain water first

distractorExplanations.a: Water conducts current across the chest and toward rescuers, so the chest must be dried first.
distractorExplanations.b: Leaving the victim in standing water risks shocking rescuers; move to a dry area first.
distractorExplanations.d: Draining water from the lungs delays CPR and AED use and is not part of BLS.

aha-bls-provider-readiness-check-team-sp.explanation: Reduce shock hazard to rescuers by avoiding standing water; AEDs are used after reasonable drying/movement.

options.a: Rotates freely between tasks as needs arise
options.b: Takes direction from whoever is closest to the patient
options.c: Chooses a task after first seeing which roles are already covered
options.d: Knows their assignment and stays in lane unless reassigned

distractorExplanations.a: Free rotation causes gaps; members take assigned roles and switch on the leader's call.
distractorExplanations.b: Direction comes from one designated team leader, not from proximity to the patient.
distractorExplanations.c: Self-selecting roles causes gaps and duplication; the leader assigns roles.

aha-bls-provider-readiness-check-team-sp.explanation: Clear roles (compressions, airway, AED, documentation) prevent task fixation and missed compressions.

options.a: Prompting rate, depth, recoil, and pauses in real time
options.b: Analyzing the heart rhythm and advising a shock
options.c: Reporting CPR quality only at the post-event debrief
options.d: Setting the ventilation volume for the bag-mask

distractorExplanations.b: Rhythm analysis is the AED's job; feedback devices measure compression quality.
distractorExplanations.c: Feedback devices coach in real time during CPR; debrief data is a secondary use.
distractorExplanations.d: Feedback devices focus on compressions and pauses, not on setting bag-mask volume.

options.a: Ventilate through the mouth and nose as in other adults
options.b: Ventilate via the tracheostomy using appropriate interface as trained
options.c: Remove the tracheostomy tube first, then ventilate by the mouth and nose
options.d: Skip ventilation and give compression-only CPR instead

distractorExplanations.a: Breathing occurs through the stoma; mouth breaths will not reach the lungs effectively.
distractorExplanations.c: Removing the tube can close the airway; ventilate through the tracheostomy.
distractorExplanations.d: Trained providers ventilate through the stoma; skipping breaths loses oxygenation.

options.a: Remove the AED pads and sit the patient upright to help them breathe
options.b: Continue compressions for 2 more minutes to prevent re-arrest
options.c: Support airway/breathing, monitor pulse, and prepare for ALS care
options.d: Give sips of water once the patient begins to respond to voice

distractorExplanations.a: Pads stay on after ROSC because re-arrest is common and may need another shock.
distractorExplanations.b: Compressions on a patient with a pulse are not indicated; monitor and support instead.
distractorExplanations.d: Oral fluids risk aspiration after ROSC; nothing by mouth while consciousness is altered.

aha-bls-provider-readiness-check-team-sp.explanation: Re-arrest is common; continue close monitoring of pulse and blood pressure as able, with supportive care, and prepare for transport/ALS care.
